extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum theorists, students and scholars of education and philosophy of education
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for organizing school studies and pedagogy so that natural sciences and humanistic studies are integrated, individual inquiry is fostered within a social context, and education advances democratic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-fertilization of natural sciences and humanistic studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should take its departure from the close interdependence of humanistic and naturalistic studies; it should aim not at keeping science as a study of nature apart from literature as a record of human interests, but at cross-fertilizing both the natural sciences and the various human disciplines such as history, literature, economics, and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogically, avoid teaching the sciences as mere technical bodies of information and humanistic studies as isolated subjects; such segregation institutes an artificial separation in the pupils' experience, breaks continuity of mental development, and deprives students of motive for interest. Instead, organize instruction so that scientific method and humanistic meaning reinforce one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ordinary experience as the pedagogical starting point for science
rubrics_metrics.description: The obvious pedagogical starting point of scientific instruction is not to teach things labeled 'science', but to utilize the familiar occupations and appliances to direct observation and experiment, until pupils have arrived at a knowledge of some fundamental principles by understanding them in their familiar practical workings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with pupils' everyday experiences (steam engines, automobiles, telegraph, household pursuits, health, street sights) and use these concrete cases to lead into principles and methods; avoid beginning with segregated, technically organized subject matter that is disconnected from daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach science in its social and human context to increase cultural value
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of scientific facts or laws in their human as well as physical and technical context enlarges their significance and gives them increased cultural value; studying science in its active incarnation is not a derogation from the 'purity' of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present scientific knowledge with its social connections and functions; economic application is incidental but part of a fact's actual connections. Emphasize function in life so that science contributes to broader cultural understanding rather than merely technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanistic study should cultivate concern for values and social well-being
rubrics_metrics.description: "Humanism" means being imbued with an intelligent sense of human interests; any study that increases concern for the values of life, produces greater sensitiveness to social well-being and greater ability to promote that well-being is humane study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing humanistic study to mere accumulation of facts (a 'miser's accumulation'); aim for imaginative enlargement of vision so that literary and historical studies react to enlarge concern for social welfare and moral interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify culture to include industry and making-a-living for democratic education
rubrics_metrics.description: A wider educational outlook would conceive industrial activities as agencies for making intellectual resources more accessible to the masses, and giving greater solidity to the culture of those having superior resources; take greater account of industry and economic conditions to overcome the separation between technical scientific studies and literary studies if society is to be truly democratic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that older humanism omitted economic and industrial conditions and tended to be aristocratic; adapting curriculum to include industrial and economic realities democratizes access to culture and prevents culture from reflecting only a ruling class's values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid philosophic dualism that separates mind and nature in education
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophic dualism between man and nature is reflected in the division of studies between the naturalistic and the humanistic; this dualism arose from certain philosophical formulations and led to treating sciences as separate technical bodies of study and literature as the repository of humanistic values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject educational schemes that institutionalize the separation of natural and humanistic studies; acknowledge continuity between man and nature (biological development, experimental method) and design curricula that embody that interdependence rather than reinforce a bifurcation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the individual: redirection and reconstruction of accepted beliefs within a social medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of the individual, or the self, in knowledge is the redirection, or reconstruction, of accepted beliefs; every new idea must have its origin in an individual but individuals develop and test ideas within a social medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage individual observation, imagination, and criticism as agencies of social progress while recognizing that individuals achieve mind and knowledge through social intercourse, shared activities, and institutional supports; do not endorse an isolated, purely private model of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat mind as purely private consciousness; emphasize social basis of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The identification of mind with the individual self as a private psychic consciousness is erroneous; the self achieves mind in the degree in which knowledge is incarnate in the life about him—the self is not a separate mind building up knowledge anew on its own account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between settled, ready-to-act 'knowledge' and the inquiring process of 'thinking'; cultivate educational practices that build shared meanings and social responsibility rather than assuming consciousnesses are intrinsically independent and unconnected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority model for moral individualism (method i)
rubrics_metrics.description: One response to moral individualism represents the survival of older authoritative positions: deviations from established belief are suspect, and certain eternal truths revealed by revelation, intuition, or tradition are set as limits to individual observation and speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educationally this model emphasizes the authority of book and teacher and discourages individual variation; it tolerates technical intellectual freedom in limited fields but reserves dogmatic limits for moral, social, legal, and political matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationalism / abstract intellectualism model (method ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: This method sets up a formal faculty of reason in distinction from tradition and concrete subject matter; reason deals with general and impersonal forms and is trusted to secure agreement between different persons' actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationalism is powerful in criticizing doctrine and in promoting clarity and order, but its formal and empty nature makes it weak in constructing new subject matter or providing specific aims and methods; educationally, it correlates to trust in general ready-made rules without ensuring pupils' ideas truly cohere with one another in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-interest / utilitarian model via commerce (method iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: English thought appealed to the intelligent self-interest of individuals to secure outer unity: legal arrangements and trade bring conduct into harmony by making individual profit depend on furnishing goods or services to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education under this model instills non-interference and some regard for others' welfare and appeals to trade and mutual benefit to align private aims with public good; it emphasizes practical interdependence (commerce) as a means of social coordination rather than purely moral authority or abstract reason.
